thread.title: The AT&T--Time Warner Deal: Financial Engineering Is Alive And Well - AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T)

author: John M. Mason
title: The AT&T--Time Warner Deal: Financial Engineering Is Alive And Well - AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T)
text:
Judge Richard J. Leon of the United States District Court in Washington declared the case presented by the US Justice Department concerning AT&T’s (NYSE: T ) acquisition of Time Warner (NYSE: TWX ) was not strong enough and the transaction should go forward. The case had been argued on “legacy” issues.
The Justice Department argued that the deal represented a “vertical” merger and this would give too much power over pricing to the “new” organization. This argument, to me, is history.
Recently, I have been writing about the “new” modern corporation. Here are two examples: “ Apple: Where the Modern Corporation is Going - II ,” and “ Renewable Energy and the "New" Modern Corporation .”
In these posts, I argued that two of the major characteristics of the “new” modern corporation are: first, they are about intangibles more than anything else, and second, they are thriving on the use of financial engineering.
The “intangibles” referred to primarily relate to intellectual property as much as anything else, but also include the use of knowledge and know-how to build sustainable competitive advantage.
The use of financial engineering is also crucial to the “new” modern corporation because, building a company upon intangibles means that the organization is capable of achieving substantial economies of scale and economies of scope.
Because of this, the “new” modern corporation generates lots and lots of cash and this resource must be used well.
One place the “new” modern corporation uses this cash is in stock buybacks . Apple, Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) has been very adept at its use of stock buybacks and has seen its stock price rise appreciably due to its financial engineering efforts.
Lots of cash and rising stock prices also serve as a foundation for mergers and acquisitions. If the foundation of the “new” modern corporation is intangibles, intellectual property, information, and consequently, is very scalable, then the “new” modern corporation has lots of ammunition to build the scale or the scope of its business.
Note, here, we are not talking about building an old-style conglomerate.
The former General Electric (NYSE: GE ) is history.
No, what we are talking about here is building networks. The physical goods and services produced become incorporated within the information networks set up by the organization. And, it is the information networks that are the framework for the performance of the corporation.
Think, for example, of what Amazon.com (NASDAQ: AMZN ) is doing. What does an Internet firm have in common with a grocery chain like Whole Foods? Information.
I am only going to cite one piece from the press today, an op-ed piece that appeared in the Wall Street Journal . This piece is titled “Godspeed to AT&T—Time Warner,” and is written by two professors at Carnegie Mellon University, Michael D. Smith and Rahul Telang.
I just want to note that the professors are not economists, but are professors of information systems. They co-direct the Initiative for Digital Entertainment Analytics.
Mr. Smith and Mr. Telang write that “in bringing the suit, the Justice Department’s antitrust chief, Makan Delrahim, argued that AT&T—Time Warner would quickly dominate the market for cable television allowing the combined behemoth to raise prices at will.”
This is the legacy argument.
The authors then ask the question “is this merger really about cable TV?”
You know the answer: “Of course not.”
Mr. Smith and Mr. Telang then talk about where the money is going in the industry. It is going “into customer connections, data analytics and back-end systems” and, they note, “these investments scale very well.”
And, the future scenario? “With any luck, AT&T and Time Warner will shortly be integrating content creation and distribution. Other companies, including Disney, probably will follow suit. That will give them leverage to compete against the tech giants (Amazon, Google, Netflix, and Facebook) that are fast becoming the dominant entertainment players."
It is all about intangibles. It is all about information.
And, this is where the “new” modern corporation is going.
